description: Malware, phishing, DoS, SQL injection and more — plus the defences that counter each threat.
content_html:
Why Cybersecurity Matters

Every connected device is a potential target. Attackers have financial, political or personal motivations to steal data, disrupt services or hold organisations to ransom. Understanding how attacks work is the first step towards defending against them. Your exam expects you to describe specific threats, explain how each works, and match it with appropriate defences.

Malware

Malware (malicious software) is a broad term covering any software designed to harm a system or its users. Key types include:

  • Virus — attaches itself to a legitimate file and spreads when that file is shared. It requires a host file and user action to propagate.
  • Worm — spreads automatically across a network without needing a host file or user action, exploiting security vulnerabilities.
  • Trojan — disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it. Once active, it can open a backdoor for an attacker.
  • Ransomware — encrypts a victim’s files and demands payment (a ransom) for the decryption key.
  • Spyware — secretly monitors user activity, capturing keystrokes, passwords and browsing habits, and sends this data to an attacker.

Phishing and Social Engineering

Phishing attacks impersonate trusted organisations — banks, delivery companies, employers — using convincing but fraudulent emails or websites. The goal is to steal login credentials, financial details or personal information.

Social engineering is the broader category that phishing belongs to. Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. Variants include:

  • Spear phishing — a targeted phishing attack aimed at a specific individual, using personal information to appear more convincing.
  • Pretexting — the attacker invents a scenario (e.g. pretending to be IT support) to gain the victim’s trust and extract information.
  • Baiting — leaving infected storage devices (e.g. USB sticks) in public places, hoping a curious person will plug one in.
Key Fact

Phishing uses deceptive emails or websites that impersonate trusted organisations to trick users into submitting passwords or financial details. It is a form of social engineering — it exploits human trust rather than technical flaws.

Brute-Force Attacks

A brute-force attack systematically tries every possible password or key until the correct one is found. Modern computers can try billions of combinations per second, making short or simple passwords easy to crack. Dictionary attacks are a faster variant that uses common words and passwords first rather than every character combination.

Denial of Service (DoS) and Distributed DoS (DDoS)

A Denial of Service (DoS) attack overwhelms a server with requests until it can no longer respond to genuine users. A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack uses a botnet — thousands of infected devices controlled by the attacker — to send traffic simultaneously, making it far harder to block because the traffic comes from many sources.

DoS/DDoS attacks target availability: the victim’s website or service becomes inaccessible. Financial services, gaming platforms and news sites are common targets.

Data Interception

Data interception (sometimes called a man-in-the-middle attack) occurs when an attacker secretly captures data travelling between two parties. On unsecured Wi-Fi networks, an attacker can intercept packets and read unencrypted data such as login credentials sent over HTTP. Using a rogue access point — a fake Wi-Fi hotspot — is one method attackers use to position themselves between a victim and the internet.

SQL Injection

SQL injection targets web applications that use databases. Many websites use SQL (Structured Query Language) to retrieve data — for example, when a user logs in, the application queries the database for matching credentials. If the input is not properly validated, an attacker can insert SQL commands into a form field to bypass authentication, extract data or delete records.

For example, entering ' OR '1'='1 as a username can trick a poorly written login query into returning all user records, granting access without a valid password.

Key Fact

The seven main threats you must know are: malware (malicious software), phishing/social engineering (psychological deception), brute-force attacks (exhaustive password guessing), DoS/DDoS (flooding a server), data interception (capturing network traffic), and SQL injection (manipulating database queries via input fields).

Defences fall into two categories: technical (software and hardware controls) and procedural (policies and user behaviour).

Anti-malware software scans files and network traffic for known malware signatures and suspicious behaviour. It must be kept up to date because new malware variants are released constantly.

Firewalls monitor incoming and outgoing network traffic and block packets that do not meet defined security rules. A firewall can block traffic from suspicious IP addresses and prevent unauthorised access to internal systems. Firewalls are the first line of defence against DoS attacks and many forms of intrusion.

User access levels limit what each user account can see and do. Principle of least privilege — granting users only the permissions they need for their role — reduces the damage if an account is compromised.

Strong passwords and two-factor authentication (2FA) defend against brute-force attacks. Long, complex passwords take vastly longer to crack; 2FA requires a second verification step (such as a code sent to a mobile device) even if the password is stolen.

Encryption protects data in transit (e.g. HTTPS/TLS) and at rest (e.g. encrypting stored files). Even if data is intercepted or a device is stolen, encrypted data cannot be read without the decryption key.

Penetration testing involves authorised security professionals deliberately attempting to break into a system to identify vulnerabilities before a real attacker does. The findings are used to patch weaknesses before they can be exploited.

Network forensics is the process of capturing and analysing network traffic logs after a security incident to determine how an attack occurred, what data was accessed and who was responsible. It supports incident response and legal proceedings.

Exam questions often ask you to match a defence to a specific threat. Use this table as a revision reference:

ThreatKey defence(s)
MalwareAnti-malware software, user access levels, email filtering
Phishing / social engineeringUser education and training, email filters, 2FA
Brute-forceStrong passwords, account lockout policies, 2FA
DoS / DDoSFirewall (traffic filtering), rate limiting, cloud-based mitigation
Data interceptionEncryption (HTTPS/TLS), VPN, avoid unsecured Wi-Fi
SQL injectionInput validation / sanitisation, parameterised queries, penetration testing
exam_tip_html: Cybersecurity questions often ask you to “describe a threat” (2–3 marks) or “explain how a named defence reduces the risk of a named threat” (4 marks). For the second type, you must link the defence directly to the mechanism of the threat. For example: “Two-factor authentication reduces the risk of brute-force attacks because even if the attacker guesses the correct password, they cannot log in without also having the second factor, such as a code sent to the victim’s phone.” Generic answers that just say “it makes it more secure” score no marks — examiners require the mechanism.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The main cybersecurity threats are malware (virus, worm, trojan, ransomware, spyware), phishing and social engineering, brute-force attacks, denial of service (DoS/DDoS), data interception and SQL injection.
  • Key defences include anti-malware software, firewalls, user access levels, strong passwords with two-factor authentication, encryption, penetration testing and network forensics.
  • To score full marks, always link a defence to the specific mechanism of the threat it counters — explain why the defence works against that particular attack.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a brute-force attack?
A) Tricking a user into revealing their password by impersonating a trusted organisation
B) Flooding a server with traffic until it cannot respond to legitimate users
C) Systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found
D) Inserting SQL commands into a form field to manipulate a database
practice_questions.marks: C) Systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a Denial of Service (DoS) attack.
practice_questions.marks: A DoS attack floods a server or network with excessive traffic so that it becomes overwhelmed and cannot respond to legitimate users. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how SQL injection can allow an attacker to bypass a login system.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- SQL injection involves entering malicious SQL code into a login form field instead of a normal username or password. [1]
- If the application does not validate or sanitise input, the SQL command is executed directly by the database. [1]
- This can trick the database into returning all user records or bypassing the password check entirely, granting access without valid credentials. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how two-factor authentication (2FA) reduces the risk of a brute-force attack being successful.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- A brute-force attack attempts to discover a password by trying every possible combination. [1]
- Even if the attacker eventually guesses the correct password, 2FA requires a second verification step, such as a one-time code sent to the user's mobile device. [1]
- The attacker does not have access to the second factor, so they cannot complete the login even with the correct password. [1]
- This makes brute-force attacks ineffective in isolation because a password alone is not sufficient to gain access. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A hospital stores sensitive patient records in a database accessible via a web portal. A security consultant has recommended penetration testing and encryption as two key defences.

Explain how each of these defences protects the hospital's data, referring to specific threats each defence counters.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation of both defences linked to specific threats (penetration testing: identifies SQL injection/authentication vulnerabilities before attackers; encryption: counters data interception and protects stolen data at rest); explicit connection between defence mechanism and the threat it counters.
Secure: Both defences explained with threat references; connection between mechanism and threat present but may lack one dimension.
Developing: Describes both defences but links to specific threats are vague or missing for one.
Emerging: Names the defences without explaining how they work.

practice_questions.text:
Cybersecurity threats are an increasing concern for individuals, businesses and governments.

Discuss the impact of cybersecurity threats on society. In your answer, consider the effects on both individuals and organisations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed impacts on individuals (financial loss, identity theft, loss of privacy, psychological harm from ransomware) and developed impacts on organisations (reputational damage, financial cost of attacks and recovery, legal liability under data protection law, disruption to critical services); may reference high-profile attack types (ransomware on NHS, DDoS on financial services); reasoned conclusion about scale and societal response.
Secure: At least two developed individual impacts and two developed organisational impacts; conclusion present.
Developing: Arguments listed on one side or the other without equal development; limited conclusion.
Emerging: Simple statements about harmful effects.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main difference between a DoS attack and a DDoS attack?
options: A DoS attack uses encryption; a DDoS attack does not
A DDoS attack uses multiple infected devices (a botnet); a DoS attack comes from one source
A DoS attack targets passwords; a DDoS attack targets databases
A DDoS attack is less powerful than a DoS attack

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of malware spreads automatically across a network without needing a host file or user action?
_____ testing involves authorised professionals attempting to break into a system to find vulnerabilities before a real attacker does.
SQL injection works by entering malicious _____ commands into a web form field, which are then executed by the database.
Match each cybersecurity threat to its primary defence:

flashcard_questions.a: Malicious software designed to disrupt, damage or gain unauthorised access to a system.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a worm differ from a virus?
flashcard_questions.a: A worm spreads automatically without a host file; a virus needs a host file and user action.

flashcard_questions.q: What does ransomware do to a victim's files?
flashcard_questions.a: It encrypts them and demands payment for the decryption key.
A deceptive email or website that impersonates a trusted organisation to steal credentials.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes spear phishing from regular phishing?
flashcard_questions.a: Spear phishing targets a specific individual, using personal information to appear convincing.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a brute-force attack try to gain access?
flashcard_questions.a: By systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a DDoS attack and how does it differ from a DoS attack?
flashcard_questions.a: DDoS uses a botnet of many infected devices; a DoS attack comes from a single source.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a rogue access point used for?
flashcard_questions.a: A fake Wi-Fi hotspot that intercepts data from devices connecting to it.

flashcard_questions.q: How does SQL injection bypass a login system?
flashcard_questions.a: Malicious SQL code in an input field tricks the database into granting access without valid credentials.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of penetration testing?
flashcard_questions.a: Authorised professionals attempt to breach a system to find vulnerabilities before attackers do.

flashcard_questions.q: What is network forensics used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Analysing network traffic logs after an attack to determine how it happened and who was responsible.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is two-factor authentication (2FA) effective against brute-force attacks?
flashcard_questions.a: Even with the correct password, the attacker cannot log in without the second factor.

glossary_terms.definition: Malicious software designed to disrupt, damage or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
A cyberattack that uses deceptive emails, websites or messages to trick users into revealing sensitive information such as passwords or financial data.
Psychological manipulation techniques used to trick people into revealing confidential information or performing actions that compromise security.
An attack that tries every possible combination of characters to guess a password or encryption key.
An attack that floods a server or network with so much traffic that it becomes overwhelmed and unable to respond to legitimate requests.
A fake wireless access point set up by an attacker to intercept data from devices that connect to it, believing it to be a legitimate network.
An attack where malicious SQL code is inserted into an input field to manipulate a database, allowing an attacker to read, modify or delete data.
